Importing, processing, and exploring Xenium data

Data Lab for ALSF

2026

Objectives

  • Read Xenium data into R
  • Calculate quality control measures on imaging spatial transcriptomic data
  • Remove likely low-quality spots with SpaceTrooper()
  • Normalize spatial expression data

Introduction

Xenium is 10x Genomics’ imaging-based in situ platform. Unlike sequencing-based methods such as single-cell RNA-seq or Visium, Xenium does not sequence anything. Instead, it measures a targeted panel of a few hundred genes directly inside intact tissue by repeated rounds of fluorescence imaging, then computationally decodes those images into individual transcript molecules.

There are two big differences to be aware of when processing Xenium data:

  • Resolution is subcellular. Each detected transcript has an (x, y, z) location in the tissue, and transcripts are assigned to individual cells identified by image segmentation. So the columns of our data are cells, not the multi-cell spots you get with Visium.

  • The gene set is fixed and small. We only measure the genes on the panel (here, 313 genes), so we can’t discover expression of genes that weren’t targeted, but we get very high sensitivity and spatial precision for the ones we do measure.

In this notebook we read in a Xenium human breast cancer dataset (the Janesick et al. dataset), compute quality-control metrics, remove low-quality cells, and normalize the expression values.

Set up

To begin, we’ll load SpatialExperiment, the core package for spatial transcriptomic objects in Bioconductor, as well as some packages for plotting.

# The main class we use for spatial transcriptomic data
library(SpatialExperiment)

# To support plotting
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Set ggplot2 theme
theme_set(theme_bw())

Directories and files

Xenium data comes as an output bundle produced by the Xenium Onboard Analysis (XOA) pipeline. The specific files present will depend on the Xenium software version and assay, but they are all described in detail in the 10x Genomics documentation.

We’ve placed the Xenium output bundle for this breast cancer sample in the directory data/brca-xenium/xenium, organized as XOA returns it.

We also have an annotations file containing cell type annotations from the original publication.

We’ll define the path to both the Xenium output and the annotations file here.

# main data directory for this sample
data_dir <- file.path("data/brca-xenium")

# directory with xenium output
xenium_outs_dir <- file.path(data_dir, "xenium")

# cell type annotations file
annotations_file <- file.path(data_dir, "Janesick_annotations.tsv")

And now, we’ll define the output paths and files we’ll use for exporting.

# Directory and file to save output
normalized_dir <- file.path(data_dir, "normalized")

# create the directory if it does not exist
fs::dir_create(normalized_dir)

# output RDS file for normalized Spatial Experiment (SPE) object
output_spe_file <- file.path(
  normalized_dir,
  "brca_xenium_normalized.rds"
)

Exploring Xenium outputs

With Visium you run Space Ranger yourself, starting from FASTQ files. Xenium is imaging-based, not sequencing-based, so there are no FASTQs. Instead, the XOA pipeline runs simultaneously on the instrument during data collection. So by the time you get data, the output is already analyzed. The instrument:

  • decoded transcripts from the images
  • segmented cells
  • assigned transcripts to cells
  • built the count matrix

Let’s look at what’s in the bundle:

Below are brief descriptions of the core files in a Xenium output bundle. Not every file is always present since it depends on the software version and the exact assay used.

experiment.xenium

A JSON file of run-level metadata: the gene panel, pixel size, software versions, and file paths. This is the entry-point file that most loaders (including the one we use below) read first.

cell_feature_matrix.h5 (and cell_feature_matrix/, cell_feature_matrix.zarr.zip)

Analogous to the feature barcode matrix output from Cell Ranger/Space Ranger.

cells.parquet / cells.csv.gz (and cells.zarr.zip)

This is the file that provides our spatial coordinates and column (cell) metadata.

transcripts.parquet / transcripts.csv.gz

This is the subcellular data that distinguishes Xenium from spot-based methods. This is analogous to the tissue_positions_list.csv for Visium.

cell_boundaries.parquet and nucleus_boundaries.parquet (plus .csv.gz versions)

The polygon vertices defining each cell’s and each nucleus’s segmentation outline.

analysis/ and analysis.zarr.zip

The instrument’s automated secondary analysis.

metrics_summary.csv and analysis_summary.html

Summary information as CSV and HTML

Morphology images (morphology.ome.tif, morphology_mip.ome.tif, morphology_focus.ome.tif / morphology_focus/)

We don’t have these to save space (as of right now), but these are the tissue morphology/DAPI images

Import with SpatialExperimentIO

We’ll import the counts and spatial information into a SpatialExperiment (SPE) object using the SpatialExperimentIO package. Note that here we are not using VisiumIO as our dataset is from Xenium, which is distinct from the previous Visium data sets we have been working with.

The only argument the function strictly requires is the path to the output bundle directory. Below we also pass a few arguments explicitly (count matrix and per-cell metadata) just so we can see what files are required, but we are still using the defaults.

By default the function also moves the Xenium control features (negative control probes, negative control codewords, unassigned codewords, etc.) out of the main gene matrix and into altExps, and adds the experiment.xenium metadata and the transcript/boundary parquet paths to metadata().

spe <- SpatialExperimentIO::readXeniumSXE(
  xenium_outs_dir,                            # path to the Xenium bundle (required)
  countMatPattern = "cell_feature_matrix.h5", # default
  metaDataPattern = "cells.parquet",          # default
  coordNames = c("x_centroid", "y_centroid")  # default; columns used as spatialCoords
)

Let’s have a look:

spe

A few things to notice about this object:

  • The dimensions show only 313 genes but roughly 167,000 cells. The gene count is small because Xenium measures a targeted panel, and because the control features have been split off into altExps (so the main matrix is genes only).
  • Each column corresponds to one cell. There are no barcodes, or spot barcodes, just cell ids.
  • The spatialCoords hold the x_centroid/y_centroid values in microns, while gene-level counts live in the counts assay.

Let’s go ahead and plot the coordinates here. Unlike with Visium, Xenium does not natively have an H&E image. This is an image that can be grabbed separately and added to the object downstream, but we won’t be working with one with this dataset.

# needed to be able to plot the coordinates with ggspavis
spe$in_tissue <- TRUE

# plot just the spots
ggspavis::plotCoords(spe)

A note on control features and altExps

A Xenium panel does not only include genes. The codebook also contains several categories of control features that let us estimate background and error rates:

  • Negative control probes target sequences that are not present in the transcriptome, so any counts reflect nonspecific probe binding (background).
  • Negative control codewords are valid codewords deliberately left unassigned to any gene, so counts reflect optical/decoding errors.
  • Other categories (unassigned/deprecated codewords, and, for some panels, genomic or antisense controls) exist too.

So we don’t mix these with real gene counts, readXeniumSXE() moves them into alternative experiments stored alongside the main object. These can be accessed with altExp.

We can see which control experiments were separated out here:

# control features are stored separately from the gene panel, as altExps
altExpNames(spe) |> 
  purrr::map(\(name) altExp(spe, name))

Add in cell type annotations

For this dataset, we have published cell type annotations, which we can join onto our object’s cell metadata.

# read the cell type annotations
cell_types_df <- readr::read_tsv(annotations_file)

The original annotations are fairly fine-grained. To make plots easier to read, we’ll collapse related labels into broader groups in a new cell_types_lumped column.

cell_types_df <- cell_types_df |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    cell_types_lumped = dplyr::case_when(
      stringr::str_detect(cell_type_annotation, "Macrophages") ~ "Macrophage",
      stringr::str_detect(cell_type_annotation, "DCIS") ~ "DCIS",
      stringr::str_detect(cell_type_annotation, "Myoepi") ~ "Myoepithelial cell",
      stringr::str_detect(cell_type_annotation, "Hybrid") ~ "Hybrid",
      stringr::str_detect(cell_type_annotation, "Tumor") ~ "Tumor",
      stringr::str_detect(cell_type_annotation, "DCs") ~ "Dendritic cell",
      .default = cell_type_annotation
    ) |>
      stringr::str_replace_all("_", " ")
  )

# check the counts of the lumped categories
cell_types_df |>
  dplyr::count(cell_types_lumped) |> 
  dplyr::arrange(desc(n))

Now we join the annotations onto the object’s colData by cell_id. Cells that are not present in the annotation file will get NA.

coldata_df <- colData(spe) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  dplyr::left_join(cell_types_df, by = "cell_id")

colData(spe) <- DataFrame(coldata_df)

To keep colors consistent across plots, we’ll build a single named palette mapping each lumped cell type to a color, and reuse it.

# build a custom palette 
cell_type_palette <- list(
  "Stromal" = "#F6222E",
  "Tumor" = "#3283FE", 
  "DCIS" = "#325A9B",
  "Macrophage" = "#85660D",
  "Myoepithelial cell" = "#F7E1A0",
  "Endothelial" = "#AA0DFE",
  "CD4+ T Cells" = "#16FF32",
  "CD8+ T Cells" = "#1C8356",
  "B Cells" = "#FC1CBF",
  "Perivascular-Like" = "#FEAF16",
  "Dendritic cell" = "#1CBE4F",
  "Mast Cells" = "#565656",
  "Unlabeled" = "grey90"
)

# unlabeled should be greyed out
cell_type_palette$Unlabeled <- "grey90"
# re-order celltypes for plotting by setting them as a factor
spe$cell_types_lumped <- as.factor(spe$cell_types_lumped) |> 
  forcats::fct_relevel(names(cell_type_palette))
# plot all spots colored by cell type 
ggspavis::plotCoords(spe, annotate = "cell_types_lumped") +
  scale_color_manual(values = cell_type_palette)

Identifying low quality spots

We use SpaceTrooper to compute per-cell quality-control metrics that are tailored to imaging-based spatial data (e.g., cell area, total counts, and control-feature counts). SpaceTrooper can be used with many different imaging based spatial transcriptomics platforms (e.g., CosMx, MERFISH). Therefore we need to specify which technology produced the data, which we set in the object’s metadata() first.

# tell SpaceTrooper which platform this is
metadata(spe)$technology <- "10X_Xenium"

# compute spatial per-cell QC metrics (adds columns like cell area, and probe counts)
# note that some of this may have been pre-calculated for this experiment but we'll re-do that here
spe <- SpaceTrooper::spatialPerCellQC(
  spe,
  use_altexps = FALSE # ignore altexps as we won't use these
)

spatialPerCellQC() writes the centroid coordinates into colData as x_centroid/y_centroid. Because spatialCoords() already holds columns with those exact names, ggspavis errors on the duplicated names when it assembles its plotting data frame. We drop the colData copies (the coordinates still live safely in spatialCoords):

# remove the duplicated coordinate columns from colData to avoid a name
# collision with spatialCoords when plotting
colData(spe) <- colData(spe) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  dplyr::select(-c("x_centroid", "y_centroid")) |>
  DataFrame()

Low-quality cells tend to be outliers in the relationship between total counts and cell area. Cells with very few counts for their area are often debris or segmentation artifacts. Below we can color the cells by these QC metrics.

p1 <- ggspavis::plotCoords(spe, annotate = "total") +
  ggplot2::scale_color_distiller(palette = "Blues", direction = 1)
Scale for colour is already present.
Adding another scale for colour, which will replace the existing scale.
p2 <- ggspavis::plotCoords(spe, annotate = "Area_um") +
  scale_color_viridis_c() +
  ggplot2::scale_color_distiller(palette = "YlOrRd", direction = 1)
Scale for colour is already present.
Adding another scale for colour, which will replace the existing scale.

We’ll then calculate outliers by finding the ratio between total counts and area and getting the threshold for three median absolute deviations (MADs) below the median.

# counts-per-area ratio for each cell
count_area_ratio <- spe$total / spe$Area_um

# flag cells that are outliers on the low side
# (3 median absolute deviations below the median, on the log2 scale since the metric is a ratio)
outliers <- scater::isOutlier(count_area_ratio, log = TRUE, type = "lower", nmads = 3)

Filtering low quality spots

Now we can filter.

In addition to the counts-per-area outliers, we use the control features as a quality signal. A high-quality cell should have essentially no control counts. Any counts in these categories indicate background or errors in that cell, so we exclude cells with a nonzero count in either control category.

# a cell is excluded if it is a counts-per-area outlier OR has any control counts
exclude <- outliers |
  spe$control_probe_counts > 0 |
  spe$control_codeword_counts > 0

# fraction of cells flagged for removal
sum(exclude) / length(exclude)
[1] 0.1573908
# store the flag and visualize which cells will be excluded
spe$exclude <- exclude

ggspavis::plotCoords(spe, annotate = "exclude") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 4))) +
  # add custom colors so excluded cells are easy to see
  scale_color_manual(values = c("grey90", "#00274C"))

# keep only the cells not flagged for removal
filtered_spe <- spe[, !spe$exclude]

dim(filtered_spe)
[1]    313 140179

Normalization

Following the recommendations in OSTA, we’ll use a simple library-size normalization. This is the same normalization we would use for Visium data.

# calculate per-spot size factors
normalized_spe <- scuttle::computeLibraryFactors(filtered_spe)

# perform normalization
normalized_spe <- scuttle::logNormCounts(normalized_spe)

Export

readr::write_rds(normalized_spe, output_spe_file)
